+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                      STRUCTURALISM MAP                                |
|                                                                       |
|  SAUSSURE (foundation)          PRAGUE SCHOOL (linguistics)           |
|  Language as system of          Trubetzkoy: phonology as              |
|  differences. Langue/parole.    system of oppositions.                |
|  Synchronic priority.           Jakobson: functions of                |
|                                 language; poetic function.            |
|         ↓                                ↓                            |
|  [FRENCH STRUCTURALISM]         [PRAGUE CONTRIBUTIONS]                |
|  Lévi-Strauss: myth,            Phoneme = distinctive unit            |
|  kinship as binary              Marked/unmarked opposition            |
|  oppositions                    Jakobson's 6 functions                |
|  Barthes: cultural signs        Foregrounding in poetics              |
|  fashion system                 Functional sentence perspective       |
|  Lacan: unconscious structured as language                            |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+

TRUBETZKOY's key insight (Grundzüge der Phonologie, 1939):
  A phoneme is defined by its OPPOSITIONS to other phonemes.
  It has no positive content — only relational value.

  (This is pure Saussure applied to phonological level.)

  /p/ in English is defined by:
  - Not /b/ (same place, voiced vs voiceless)
  - Not /t/ (same voiceless stop, different place)
  - Not /k/ (same voiceless stop, different place)
  - Not /f/ (same voiceless labial, fricative vs stop)
  - etc.

  DISTINCTIVE FEATURES (Jakobson & Halle):
  Phonemes are bundles of binary features.
  [+voice] / [-voice]
  [+nasal] / [-nasal]
  [+labial] / [-labial]
  [+strident] / [-strident]

  /p/ = [-voice, -nasal, +labial, -strident, +stop]
  /b/ = [+voice, -nasal, +labial, -strident, +stop]

  All phonemes in all languages from a small set of binary features.
  This is the prototypical application of binary opposition to structure.

Every communicative act involves six factors:

                      CONTEXT
                    (Referential ─ orientation toward world/topic)
                          │
  ADDRESSER ────── MESSAGE ────── ADDRESSEE
  (Emotive         (Poetic          (Conative
   function:        function:        function:
   expresses        oriented         oriented
   sender's         toward the       toward
   inner state,     form of the      addressee;
   attitude)        message          "Come here!",
                    itself;          imperatives,
                    foregrounding    appeals,
                    of form)         "you" forms)
                          │
                      CONTACT
                    (Phatic ─ maintaining the channel:
                     "Hello?", "you know what I mean?",
                     "uh-huh", "are you still there?")
                          │
                        CODE
                    (Metalingual ─ about the code itself:
                     "What do you mean by X?",
                     "Define your terms",
                     a grammar is metalingual about language)

  PRIMARY FUNCTION = the one that dominates in a given text.
  A message may have all six simultaneously.

BINARY OPPOSITION AND MARKED/UNMARKED ↔ TYPE SYSTEMS AND DEFAULTS

BINARY OPPOSITION:
  Structuralism's claim: meaning in a system is generated by
  binary contrasts between terms (voiced/unvoiced, raw/cooked,
  nature/culture). Neither term has meaning in isolation;
  meaning is the difference.
  Formal analog: Boolean logic. True/False have no meaning
  except through their opposition. The binary is the primitive
  unit of distinction — one bit of information.

MARKED / UNMARKED ↔ DEFAULT VALUES:
  The unmarked term is the DEFAULT — used in neutral contexts,
  no special marking required.
  The marked term requires explicit specification — it signals
  departure from the default.
  Type system examples:
    bool: false is unmarked (zero value in Go, C#, Java);
          true is marked (requires explicit assertion)
    nullable types: T is unmarked; T? is marked (nullable reference types in C#)
    Non-nullable: string is unmarked; string? requires explicit marking
    Default constructors: the default constructor produces the
      unmarked value; non-default constructors produce marked instances.

  Database NULL semantics:
    NULL is the marked value — it requires special handling,
    special operators (IS NULL, COALESCE), and special semantics.
    A non-NULL value is the unmarked default.
    Three-valued logic (T/F/NULL) is the formal consequence of
    introducing a marked third term to the binary.

  API design:
    Optional parameters have unmarked defaults.
    Providing a value marks the choice as intentional.
    When you add a default to a function parameter, you are
    declaring that value as the unmarked case.

PROPP'S FUNCTIONS ↔ STATE MACHINE:
  Propp identifies 31 narrative functions in fixed order.
  Not all functions appear in every tale, but those that do
  appear always in the same sequence.
  Formal model: a state machine with 31 states, where valid
  transitions are the narrative logic (villainy → heroresponse
  → journey → test → victory → return).
  Not all paths are taken; some states can be skipped.
  The machine is deterministic at the level of function sequence —
  which is what Propp means by "morphology."
